content: The studies reviewed included interventions that were either placebo-controlled or non-pharmacological, such as behavioral interventions, acupressure, or fennel extract. Eighteen studies compared one pharmaceutical agent to another, and one additional study included both an active drug and a placebo arm. Most of the studies originated from high-income countries, with only one study conducted in a lower-middle-income country (Pakistan) and none from low-income countries. There were very few studies available for each drug class. One study evaluated the effects of the anticonvulsant pregabalin compared to placebo. It reported a beneficial effect on pain intensity and patient global impression of change post-treatment, but the evidence was of very low certainty. There were no significant effects on achieving 30% or 50% pain reduction or on sleep post-treatment, with all evidence being of very low certainty. Six studies compared antidepressants to placebo. There was no significant difference in pooled outcomes for pain intensity post-treatment or at follow-up, with evidence ranging from low to very low certainty. One study reported benefits for achieving 30% and 50% pain reduction post-intervention, but the evidence was of very low certainty. Another small study noted improvements in health-related quality of life post-treatment and at follow-up with antidepressants, but again, the evidence was of very low certainty. No effects were observed on functional disability, anxiety, depression, activity participation, or patient satisfaction post-treatment or at follow-up, with evidence ranging from low to very low certainty. A single study compared NSAIDs to acupressure and found no difference in pain intensity post-treatment, with very low certainty evidence. Few adverse events were reported in the randomized controlled trials (RCTs) included in this review. Treatment groups experienced more adverse events than controls, but the differences were not statistically significant, except in one study comparing duloxetine (an antidepressant) to placebo, where significantly more treatment-related adverse effects were observed in the treatment group. However, the evidence was of very low certainty. The small size of the included RCTs may have limited their ability to detect statistically significant differences in less common adverse events. Seventy-four studies met the inclusion criteria for acceptability and feasibility assessments, with 33 selected for detailed evaluation. Of these, 18 focused on specific interventions within the scope of the guidelines, including 12 linked to trials in the effectiveness systematic review. All 18 studies were conducted in high-income countries and included physical therapy, psychological interventions, and mixed interventions. No studies examined pharmacological therapies. Few studies focused on children under eight years of age. In lowor middle-income settings, 15 additional studies were identified, but these did not examine specific pain interventions. Instead, they provided data on attitudes and barriers to pain management in children. Most of the 33 studies had significant methodological limitations. The analysis identified perceived benefits and harms of physical and psychological therapies. Physical therapies were associated with increased physical activity, lower perceived pain intensity, and increased energy, but also with increased pain during and after exercise, family distress, conflict, child non-adherence, exhaustion, and time burdens on parents. Psychological therapies were perceived to improve sleep, mood, quality of life, and family communication, and to reduce anxiety. Group formats were sometimes supportive but could be unsuitable for mixed-severity pain conditions without skilled facilitation. Barriers to interventions included unappealing content, reluctance to practice skills in front of peers, and mismatches between intervention outcomes and family expectations. Facilitators included personal relevance, tailored content, and prior positive experiences with effective interventions. Broader barriers to optimal pain management included poverty, limited access to care, sociocultural norms, lack of expertise and training in pediatric pain management, and insufficient pediatric healthcare services. Three studies focused on cost-effectiveness, all conducted in high-income countries. One study evaluated an intensive interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation program, reporting improved pain outcomes and cost savings due to reduced healthcare utilization. Two studies examined internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) interventions, with no significant cost differences between intervention groups. No studies were identified that compared costs across multiple intervention types. Cost estimates included only intervention delivery and excluded downstream effects such as reduced healthcare utilization or parental work leave. The guidelines emphasize that access to pain management is a fundamental human right, as recognized by international human rights instruments. States have an obligation to ensure access to essential medicines for pain relief. Children have the right to the highest attainable standard of health, as outlined in the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child. Member states and healthcare providers should ensure that children and their families are aware of their rights, enabling them to advocate for appropriate care. Best practices for managing chronic pain in children include adopting a biopsychosocial approach, recognizing pain as a multidimensional experience influenced by biological, psychological, and social factors. Comprehensive assessments should inform pain management plans, using ageand culturally appropriate tools to monitor pain intensity and its impact on quality of life. Children with chronic pain should receive thorough evaluations for underlying conditions and access to appropriate treatments. Management should be tailored to the child’s health, developmental age, abilities, and social and emotional needs, and care should be childand family-centered. Interdisciplinary, multimodal approaches are recommended, incorporating physical, psychological, and pharmacological interventions as appropriate. Opioid stewardship is essential, ensuring opioids are used only for appropriate indications, with careful monitoring and clear plans for continuation or discontinuation. Families must receive timely and accurate information, with shared decision-making and clear communication tailored to their needs. Comprehensive care should address all aspects of the child’s development and well-being, including educational, cultural, and social needs.
